To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the liver is not injured by long-term alcohol consumption in rats.
Alcoholic beverages, when given in amounts that cause intoxication, are not more harmful to the rat liver than an isocaloric amount of glucose, even in combination with an inadequate diet.

the effect of ethanol on liver is dependent on the type of diet, and that ethanol has a hepatoprotective effect on rats with a low-protein diet, but a hepatotoxic effect on rats with an adequate diet.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effect of different alcoholic beverages on the rat liver when given in combination with inadequate diets, and with the influence of the different alcoholic beverages on vitamin A metabolism in rats and man.
the effect of long-term alcohol consumption on the liver of rats, and the effect of the alcohol type and of the nutritional status on this process.
the effects on the rat liver and the blood of long-term administration (several months) of alcoholic beverages (gin, brandy, whiskey, red wine) together with different diets.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of ethanol in the rat are largely independent of its source, and that the effects of alcohol on the liver are largely independent of the nutritional background.
the liver is not particularly vulnerable to ethanol, but is more vulnerable to the effects of malnutrition, especially of protein and vitamins.
the liver lesions in rats are due to the alcohol and not to the congener.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the rat, long-term alcohol administration is not hepatotoxic, but the diet is.

in spite of a high mortality rate no significant liver lesions occurred, and that in spite of the fact that the rats given alcohol were in a bad nutritional state, they were able to compensate for the alcohol and the nutritional inadequacy, and that the liver function remained normal.
the liver damage in alcoholics is due to the alcoholic beverage per se rather than to the ethanol content.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the liver is very good at adapting to different types of alcoholic beverages and diets.
alcohol consumption is not the only factor in the development of liver disease.
alcohol is not the only factor that contributes to liver cirrhosis.
